title: Egmont Overture
hook: Eight and a half minutes from a tyrant’s heavy tread to a hero’s death and a blaze of victory, written for Goethe’s play.

painting.title: The Last Moments of Count Egmont
painting.pairingNote: Gallait shows Egmont in his last hours, gazing out of a window while a bishop waits beside him; the overture’s closing minutes pass from this hour to his death and turn it into victory.

facts: In 1810 the court theatre in Vienna, the Burgtheater, revived *Egmont*, the tragedy Johann Wolfgang von Goethe finished in 1787 and published in 1788, and asked Beethoven for the music: an overture and nine numbers for songs, interludes and the final scene. He had begun sketching it by the autumn of 1809. It was not ready for the opening night on 24 May 1810; his music was first heard at the fourth performance, on 15 June.

The play is about a real man. Lamoral, Count of Egmont, a nobleman of the Low Countries, stood up against the harsh rule of Spain. The Duke of Alba, sent by King Philip II, had him arrested, and he was beheaded in the main square of Brussels on 5 June 1568. His death helped start the revolt that led to the independence of the Netherlands.

In Goethe’s play Egmont goes to his death unbroken, and the drama ends with what Goethe calls a “victory symphony”. Beethoven, who revered Goethe, wrote that he had composed the music “purely out of love for the poet” and took no fee from the theatre.
The overture soon led a life of its own. Breitkopf & Härtel printed it separately in December 1810, well before the rest of the music, and it has been a concert favourite ever since.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a slow, heavy dance of oppression, a fierce fight in quick triple time, a sudden death, a hush, and a victory march in the major.

movements.heading: Sostenuto, ma non troppo – Allegro – Allegro con brio
movements.tempo: Sostenuto, ma non troppo – Allegro – Allegro con brio
movements.summary: One movement in three parts. A slow introduction sets heavy, stamping chords against sad woodwind sighs. A fast section in [[sonata-form|sonata form]] tells of struggle. Then, after a single crushing blow and a silence, the music turns from F minor to F major and ends in a brilliant victory march.

mainIdeas.name: The tread
mainIdeas.description: loud, heavy string chords with the weight on the second beat, the rhythm of a slow [[sarabande|sarabande]], a dance of Spanish origin. It is often heard as the power of Spain.

mainIdeas.name: The sighs
mainIdeas.description: quiet, falling phrases in oboe, clarinet and bassoon answering the chords, like voices of complaint.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1 of the Allegro
mainIdeas.description: a falling, restless line that starts in the cellos and is passed up to the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The victory music
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, rustling figure in the strings that grows into fanfares for horns and trumpets, with the shrill piccolo on top.

stops.hear: The whole orchestra strikes one long, loud note; then slow, heavy chords in the strings
stops.happening: The introduction. The stamping chords move in the rhythm of a [[sarabande|sarabande]]

stops.hear: Soft woodwinds answer the chords with sad, falling sighs
stops.happening: Oppression and complaint, side by side

stops.hear: A small falling figure in the violins repeats, getting louder and faster
stops.happening: The introduction speeds up into the Allegro

stops.hear: Quick and urgent: the cellos start a restless, falling tune and the violins take it up
stops.happening: Theme 1 of the [[exposition|exposition]], in F minor

stops.hear: The full orchestra, loud, with hard accents
Loud, blunt string chords, each answered by a gentle phrase in the woodwinds
stops.happening: Theme 2, in A-flat major: the slow dance of the introduction, now fast

stops.hear: Short pieces of the main tune tossed between strings and woodwinds
The restless cello tune returns at the start
The blunt chords and gentle woodwind answers come back in a new key
The music drives on, louder and more and more tense
The heavy dance rhythm crashes out once more; one violent stroke, then silence
Very soft, slow chords in the woodwinds, almost still
stops.happening: A pause between death and victory

stops.hear: A quiet rustling in the strings rises and swells; F major breaks through
stops.happening: The *Allegro con brio*: the victory music that also ends Goethe’s play

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: Horn and trumpet fanfares, the piccolo shrieking above, hammered chords
stops.happening: The [[coda|coda]], loud to the last bar

notice: Listen for the silence after the violent stroke near the end. Everything stops, and then the soft woodwind chords begin, as if the music were holding its breath.
Compare the opening chords with Theme 2 of the Allegro. Theme 2 is the same heavy dance rhythm, only faster.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: George Szell made the Cleveland Orchestra famous for its precision. He recorded the overture in Severance Hall in October 1966, during the years in which he also recorded all nine Beethoven symphonies with the orchestra.

threads.title: Freedom
threads.body: Beethoven wrote the music in 1809–10, the year Napoleon’s army occupied Vienna. A play about a man who dies resisting a foreign power had a clear meaning for its audience.

threads.title: Death turned into victory
threads.body: The overture ends in the major and at full force: the hero is dead, but his cause wins. Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony, finished two years earlier, also moves from struggle in a minor key to triumph in the major.

threads.title: Goethe
threads.body: Beethoven asked his publisher to send Goethe the score and wrote to the poet himself in April 1811. The two men met in the summer of 1812 at the spa town of Teplitz.
